title: Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI): Generic Syntax
summary: Defines the generic grammar of Uniform Resource Identifiers, the strings such as web addresses that name resources. It lets software split any URI into its common parts without knowing the details of each scheme. It was a draft standard, now replaced by RFC 3986.

plainLanguage.summary:
A URI is a short string of characters that names something: a web page, a file, a mailbox, a newsgroup. This RFC gives the shape that all of them share, so a program can pull a URI apart before it knows what kind of URI it is.

It also explains the percent sign, the way characters that cannot appear directly are written as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits.

subtitle: The generic grammar that lets software split any web address or other identifier into its common parts.

tldr.problem: Every kind of web address and name has its own layout, but software often has to read one without knowing which kind it is, or has to combine a short reference with a longer one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a grammar for the parts every identifier shares: a scheme, an optional authority, a path and an optional query. It also defines how characters outside that set are escaped and how a relative reference is resolved against a base address.
tldr.outcome: It was a Draft Standard and was later replaced by RFC 3986. At the time it merged and updated RFC 1738 and RFC 1808 into one generic syntax.

facts.label: Escape sequence length
facts.value: 3 characters: a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits

facts.label: Characters allowed in a scheme name
facts.value: A lower case letter, then lower case letters, digits, plus, period or hyphen

today: RFC 2396 was a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3986, which revised the generic URI syntax. When it was published it merged and updated RFC 1738 and RFC 1808 into a single generic syntax for all URIs.

sections.title: What a URI Is
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier is a compact string of characters for identifying an abstract or physical resource. The RFC characterises URIs through three ideas. Uniformity lets different types of resource identifier be used in the same context even when the mechanisms for reaching them differ, lets common syntactic conventions be interpreted the same way across types, lets new types be introduced without disturbing existing ones, and lets the same identifiers be reused in many contexts, so new applications can rely on a large existing set. A resource is anything that has identity: an electronic document, an image, a service such as today's weather report for a city, or a collection of other resources. Not all resources are retrievable over the network; people, companies and library books are resources too. The resource is the conceptual mapping to an entity or set of entities, not necessarily the entity at any particular moment, so a resource can stay the same while its content changes. An identifier is an object that can act as a reference to something with identity; for a URI that object is a sequence of characters with a restricted syntax.

A URI can be classified as a locator, a name, or both. A URL, the Uniform Resource Locator, is the subset of URI that identify a resource through a representation of its primary access mechanism, such as its network location. A URN, the Uniform Resource Name, is the subset of URI that are required to remain globally unique and persistent even when the resource ceases to exist or becomes unavailable.

The scheme defines the namespace of the URI and may restrict the syntax and semantics further. This specification defines the elements of the URI syntax that are required of all schemes or common to many, so that a scheme-independent parser can parse the common components and leave scheme-dependent handling until it is needed. Although many URL schemes are named after protocols, this does not imply that the named protocol is the only way to reach the resource, and resolving one URL may need more than one protocol, for example both DNS and HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Three words carry the idea: uniform so that everything can be handled the same way, resource so that a name can point at a thing, and identifier so that the name is a compact string you can write down and pass around.

sections.title: Characters and Escape Sequences
sections.content:
URIs consist of a restricted set of characters, primarily chosen to aid transcribability and usability in computer systems and in non-computer communication. Characters conventionally used as delimiters around URIs were excluded, and the set that remains is digits, letters and a few graphic symbols common to most character encodings and input facilities available to Internet users. The syntax was designed with global transcribability as a main concern: a URI is a sequence of characters from a very limited set, so it can be written on a napkin and typed into a computer later, and its meaning depends only on the characters used and not on how they are represented.

Within a URI, characters are either used as delimiters or represent strings of data within the delimited portions. The reserved characters, which are allowed in a URI but limited to their reserved purpose, are ;, /, ?, :, @, &, =, +, $ and ,. They are not reserved in every context; the set actually reserved in a given component is defined by that component, and in general a character is reserved if the semantics of the URI change when it is replaced with its escaped form. The unreserved characters, which have no reserved purpose, are upper and lower case letters, decimal digits, and a limited set of punctuation marks and symbols: hyphen, underscore, period, exclamation mark, tilde, asterisk, apostrophe, and the two parentheses. Escaping an unreserved character does not change the meaning of the URI, but it should not be done unless the context does not allow the character to appear unescaped.

Data must be escaped if it has no representation using an unreserved character. An escaped octet is encoded as a character triplet: the percent character followed by the two hexadecimal digits representing the octet code, so %20 is the escaped encoding for the space character. Because the percent character always has the reserved purpose of being the escape indicator, it must itself be written as %25 in order to be used as data. Implementers should be careful not to escape or unescape the same string more than once, since unescaping an already unescaped string might lead to misinterpreting a percent data character as another escaped character.

Several US-ASCII characters are excluded. The control characters, 00-1F and 7F, are excluded because they are non-printable and likely to be misinterpreted by control mechanisms. The space is excluded because significant spaces may disappear and insignificant ones may be introduced during transcription, and because whitespace delimits URIs in many contexts. The angle brackets, the double quote and the percent sign are excluded because they are used as delimiters or for encoding. A further set, {, }, |, \, ^, [, ] and `, is excluded because gateways and other transport agents are known to sometimes modify such characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a short list of characters is allowed directly. Anything else, including a space, is written as a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, so the URI stays safe to copy between systems.

sections.title: The Four Components
sections.content:
The URI syntax depends on the scheme. In general an absolute URI is written as <scheme>:<scheme-specific-part>, where the scheme-specific part has no structure or semantics common to all URIs. A subset of URIs does share a common syntax for hierarchical relationships within a namespace, and that generic syntax consists of four main components: <scheme>://<authority><path>?<query>, each of which except the scheme may be absent. Some schemes do not allow an authority component and others do not use a query component. URIs that do not use the slash to separate hierarchical components are considered opaque by the generic URI parser.

The scheme comes first and defines the semantics for the rest of the string. Scheme names begin with a lower case letter followed by any combination of lower case letters, digits, plus, period or hyphen. For resiliency, programs should treat upper case letters as equivalent to lower case in scheme names, so that HTTP and http both work.

The authority is the top hierarchical element for a naming authority, typically an Internet-based server or a scheme-specific registry. It is preceded by a double slash and terminated by the next slash, the question mark, or the end of the URI. It is either a server-based authority or a registry-based one. The server form is <userinfo>@<host>:<port>, where the user information and the port may both be omitted. The host is a domain name or an IPv4 address written as four decimal groups separated by periods; literal IPv6 addresses are not supported, and a suitable representation for them is desired but has not yet been determined. The port is the network port number for the server, and when it is omitted the default port for the scheme is assumed. Some URL schemes use the format user:password in the user information field, and the RFC says this is not recommended, because passing authentication information in clear text has proven to be a security risk in almost every case where it has been used.

The path contains data specific to the authority, identifying the resource within the scope of that scheme and authority. It may consist of path segments separated by a single slash, and each segment may include parameters introduced by a semicolon. The query is a string of information to be interpreted by the resource.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part says which kind of name this is. The rest, after the double slash, says who is in charge and which thing under them is meant.

sections.title: Relative References and Their Resolution
sections.content:
Some URI schemes support a hierarchical naming system, where a slash separates the components of the name. The document defines a scheme-independent relative form that can be used with a base URI to produce another URI. An absolute identifier refers to a resource independently of the context in which it is used, while a relative identifier refers to a resource by describing the difference within a hierarchical namespace between the current context and an absolute identifier.

The base URI is established according to the rules in the RFC, which cover a base URI within document content, one from the entity that encapsulates the document, one from the retrieval URI, and a default base URI. It is then parsed into the four main components. Only the scheme component is required to be present; the others may be empty or undefined, and a component is undefined if its preceding separator does not appear. The base URI's query component is not used by the resolution algorithm and may be discarded.

The resolution algorithm then works through the reference in order. The reference is parsed into its potential components and fragment identifier. If the path is empty and the scheme, authority and query components are undefined, it is a reference to the current document. If the scheme is defined, the reference is an absolute URI. Otherwise the scheme is inherited from the base URI. If the authority is defined, the reference is a network-path reference; otherwise the authority is inherited from the base URI. If the path begins with a slash the reference is an absolute-path reference. Otherwise the reference is a relative-path reference, and its path is merged with the base URI's path: all but the last segment of the base path are copied to a buffer, the reference path is appended, and then the buffer is cleaned up by removing ./ segments, removing <segment>/../ patterns iteratively from the left, and removing a trailing <segment>/... If the result still begins with complete path segments of .., the reference is in error.
sections.plainLanguage: A short name such as one dot dot slash is finished off against the address it was found in, so the program works out the whole address before doing anything with it.

sections.title: Normalization and Equivalence
sections.content:
In many cases different URI strings identify the identical resource. The host names used in URL are case insensitive, so http://www.XEROX.com is equivalent to http://www.xerox.com. In general the rules for equivalence and for the definition of a normal form are scheme dependent. When a scheme uses elements of the common syntax, it will also use the common syntax equivalence rules: the scheme and the hostname are case insensitive, and a URL with an explicit port, where the port is the default for the scheme, is equivalent to one where the port is left out.

The RFC also states that a URI is always in an escaped form, since escaping or unescaping a completed URI might change its semantics. Normally the only time escape encodings can safely be made is when the URI is being created from its component parts, because each component may have its own set of reserved characters, and only the mechanism responsible for generating or interpreting that component can tell whether not escaping a character will change its meaning. In the same way, a URI must be separated into its components before the escaped characters within them can be safely decoded. If the scheme defines a canonicalization algorithm, unreserved characters may be unescaped according to it, so %7e is sometimes used instead of ~ in an http URL path even though the two are equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: Two spellings of the same address are often the same address. The rules for deciding that are mostly left to each kind of address, with a few shared rules about case and about the default port.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A URI does not in itself pose a security threat. Users should be aware that there is no general guarantee that a URL, which at one time located a given resource, will continue to do so, and no guarantee that a URL will not locate a different resource later, because there is no constraint on how a given authority apportions its namespace. Such a guarantee can only be obtained from the people controlling that namespace and the resource in question.

It is sometimes possible to construct a URL such that an attempt to perform a seemingly harmless, idempotent operation, such as retrieving an entity associated with the resource, will in fact cause a possibly damaging remote operation to occur. The unsafe URL is typically constructed by specifying a port number other than the one reserved for the network protocol in question, so the client unwittingly contacts a site running a different protocol, and the content of the URL contains instructions that, when interpreted according to that other protocol, cause an unexpected operation. An example has been the use of a gopher URL to cause an unintended or impersonating message to be sent via an SMTP server. Caution should be used with any URL that specifies a port number other than the default for the protocol, especially one within the reserved space.

Care should also be taken that a URL containing escaped delimiters for a given protocol, for example the CR and LF characters for telnet, is not unescaped before transmission, because that could let characters simulate an extra operation or parameter and cause an unexpected remote operation. Finally, it is clearly unwise to use a URL that contains a password intended to be secret, and the use of a password within the user information component is strongly disrecommended except where the password is intended to be public.
sections.plainLanguage: The address itself is not dangerous, but where it points can change, and pointing it at a different port can make a harmless request do something else entirely.

viz.caption: The collected grammar from Appendix A of RFC 2396

data.title: URI grammar
data.code:
URI-reference = [ absoluteURI | relativeURI ] [ "#" fragment ]
absoluteURI   = scheme ":" ( hier_part | opaque_part )
relativeURI   = ( net_path | abs_path | rel_path ) [ "?" query ]
hier_part     = ( net_path | abs_path ) [ "?" query ]
opaque_part   = uric_no_slash *uric
net_path      = "//" authority [ abs_path ]
abs_path      = "/"  path_segments
rel_path      = rel_segment [ abs_path ]
path          = [ abs_path | opaque_part ]
path_segments = segment *( "/" segment )
segment       = *pchar *( ";" param )
param         = *pchar
pchar         = unreserved | escaped | ":" | "@" | "&" | "=" | "+" | "$" | ","
authority     = server | reg_name
server        = [ [ userinfo "@" ] hostport ]
userinfo      = *( unreserved | escaped | ";" | ":" | "&" | "=" | "+" | "$" | "," )
hostport      = host [ ":" port ]
host          = hostname | IPv4address
port          = *digit
query         = *uric
fragment      = *uric

viz.caption: The classes of character a URI is built from

items.title: Unreserved
items.text: Letters, digits and the marks - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ). They carry no special meaning and can be escaped without changing the URI.

items.title: Reserved
items.text: The characters ; / ? : @ & = + $ and ,. They delimit parts of the URI and are reserved only in the components that use them.

items.title: Escaped
items.text: A percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits, standing for one octet. %20 is a space and %25 is a percent sign.

items.title: Excluded
items.text: Control characters, the space, the delimiters < > " # %, and the unwise set { } | \ ^ [ ] `, which gateways sometimes alter.

viz.caption: How a URI, a URL and a URN relate

cells: The subset that identifies a resource by a representation of its primary access mechanism
The subset required to stay globally unique and persistent even when the resource ceases to exist
The generic syntax defined by this RFC

A URN is a kind of URI, drawn from a set of defined namespaces
The scheme, then the authority, the path and the query
The urn scheme is reserved for standardized URN namespaces
